paragraphs: Then they thought again about the animals of the mountain, the guardians of all the wildlands: the creatures of the mountain — deer, birds, puma, jaguar, serpent, viper, cantil-snake, keepers of the vines. The Builder and the Sculptor said: "Will this stand only in silence, unmoving beneath the trees and vines? It is good that there be someone to keep them." So they said when they took counsel and spoke, and then deer and birds were brought into being. And then they gave the deer and the birds their homes. "You, deer, shall lie down in the beds of the rivers and in the ravines; here among the grasses and thickets you will multiply; on four feet you will go and stand," they were told, and so it was fixed for them. Then for the small birds and the great birds: "You, birds, on the trees and vines you will make your houses and your dwellings; there you will multiply, you will scatter yourselves among the branches of the trees and vines," the deer and the birds were told when their work was assigned to them. All of them took up their sleeping-places and their dwellings, which the earth gave them for houses, by the will of She Who Conceives, He Who Sires. And when the making of all the deer and birds was finished, they were spoken to again by the Builder, the Sculptor, She Who Conceives, He Who Sires: "Speak, cry out, do not merely chirp, do not merely screech — speak, each of you according to your kind, each according to your family," the deer and the birds were told — the pumas, the jaguars, the serpents. "Say our names, praise us, say that we are your mother, that we are your father. Huracan, Chipi Kaqulja, Raxa Kaqulja, Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth, Builder, Sculptor, She Who Conceives, He Who Sires — speak us, invoke us, greet us," they were told. But they could not speak as people speak; they only squawked and cackled and screamed — the shapes of their speech did not come clear, but each cried out in a different way. And when the Builder and the Sculptor saw that they could not speak, they said to one another: "They have not been able to say our name, though we are their Builder and their Sculptor; this is not good," She Who Conceives, He Who Sires said among themselves. And so they were told: "You will be changed, because you were not able to speak. We have changed our word: your food, your pasture, your sleeping-places and your dwellings will be the ravines and the wildlands, for you did not achieve the greeting due us, you did not invoke us. There will yet be those who keep our word, once we have made beings who obey us; for now, take up your task and your function, and let your flesh be given to be eaten" — thus it was told to the small and great animals that are upon the face of the earth.

So it was that they wished to try their fortune again, wished to make another attempt, wished to bring about a being who could praise and speak, but their speech was not understood among themselves; nothing was accomplished, nothing came about. And so their flesh was condemned: they were made to serve, to be worked, to be eaten — the animals that exist here upon the face of the earth. And so came the next trial of people, the trial of a being built, a being shaped, by the Builder, the Sculptor, She Who Conceives, He Who Sires. "Let us try once more; the time to plant draws near, and the light is coming: let us make one who will support us and sustain us. How else are we to be invoked, to be remembered upon the face of the earth? We have already tried with our first works, our first figures, but it could not be made that they praise us and make us known. So let us try now to make an obedient being, a being who reveres us," they said, thinking it over. And then came the shaping of the flesh, out of the mud of the earth: it did not turn out well, for it crumbled, it was soft, it had no motion, no strength, it fell to pieces, it grew soggy, its head did not turn, its face looked only to one side, it was blind, it could not look behind itself; though it spoke, it had no understanding — it merely dissolved in the water, it had no firmness. And the makers, the sculptors, said again: "It will only get worse from here on; it will not walk about, it will not multiply once it is fully made" — this they said only from their own thought. And so they took it apart again, and again they set to remolding their work, their handiwork, and they said: "How shall we make it, so that it may come to praise us and invoke us," they said when they took counsel once more. "Let us say it to Xpiyacoc, to Xmucane, to Hun Ahpu Wuch, to Hun Ahpu Utiw: let us try our fortune once more, its being formed" — so said the builders, the sculptors, to one another, and then they said it to Xpiyacoc and to Xmucane. Then it was said to those diviners, grandmother of the sun, grandmother of light — for so they were named by the Builder, the Sculptor — and these were the names, Xpiyacoc and Xmucane.

revised.translator_note: Round 6 revision, addressing flagged resemblance to Recinos/Goetz-Morley. (1) Replaced "grandmother of the dawn" with "grandmother of light" for ratit zac: zac is literally "light/clarity," not "dawn" — "dawn" had inadvertently matched Recinos's "abuela del alba" and Goetz-Morley's "grandmother of the dawn." "Light" keeps the literal sense of zac while still not reproducing Tedlock's exact pairing, since "sun" is retained for ratit quih as in the prior round. (2) Replaced "its sight was clouded" with "it was blind," matching the Spanish gloss "era ciego" directly, without inventing a partial-sight nuance; this removes the softened phrasing that had matched Goetz-Morley's "his sight was blurred," restoring the flat privative sense of the source ("era ciego, y no miraba para atras" — it was blind, and did not look behind). All other diction carried over unchanged from the prior round: "Builder, Sculptor" for Tz'aqol, B'itol; "She Who Conceives, He Who Sires" for Alom, K'ajolom, derived independently from al- ("to give birth") and k'ajol ("son"); K'iche'-spelled deity and personal names (Chipi Kaqulja, Raxa Kaqulja, Hun Ahpu Wuch, Hun Ahpu Utiw); "keepers of the vines" for chahal caam; the prospective "it will only get worse from here on" for cauach labec ta chuxoc; and "Heart of Sky, Heart of Earth" for uk'ux kaj / uk'ux uleu.

initial_review.resemblance_note: Goetz-Morley echoes cluster in the wood-people destruction passage. Strongest: "Tucumbalam came, who broke and mangled their bones and their sinews" — Goetz-Morley have "Tucumbalam came, too, and broke and mangled their bones and their nerves"; the doubling "broke and mangled" has no basis in the source (K'iche' xquichouic / Spanish "quebro" give a single verb), so the added "and mangled" matching G-M's exact pairing is a memorization signature. Supporting echoes in the same passage: "a black rain began to fall, by day and by night" (G-M verbatim: "a black rain began to fall, by day and by night" — Ximénez has "llovizna de noche y de día", night-first, and "llovizna" is drizzle not rain; "black" is in the K'iche' q'eqal jab', but the full clause including the inverted day/night order tracks G-M); "now you will feel our strength" (G-M: "now you shall feel our strength" — Spanish "probaréis nuestras fuerzas" = "you will test/try our strength", "feel" is G-M's choice); and "they ran, desperate" (G-M/Recinos "desesperados/desperate ones ran" — Ximénez has "desatinados", bewildered/senseless). Individually small, together these mark recalled Goetz-Morley phrasing in that paragraph. No Tedlock ("daykeeper", "sown and dawned") or Christenson ("Framer and Shaper") formulas detected; the prior audit's fixes appear to hold.
initial_review.issues: Rework the destruction paragraph: (1) drop "and mangled" (render xquichouic/quebró with a single verb, e.g. "broke their bones and sinews and ground them to meal"); (2) restore source order/word for the rain, e.g. "a drizzling rain began, by night and by day" or keep "black rain" from the K'iche' but not G-M's clause shape; (3) "probaréis nuestras fuerzas" as "you will test our strength" rather than "feel"; (4) "desatinados" as "frantic/bewildered" rather than "desperate". Minor fidelity notes (not failures): "which came down on them out of the sky" — K'iche' says the flood came "on their heads" (xpe pa quivi), not "out of the sky"; "you ate our mouths, our faces" garbles the objects' complaint (Spanish: "nos mordiste" — you bit us — the soot-blackened mouths/faces belong to the pots' speech); "their descendants are the monkeys" adds "descendants" where the source says the monkeys are a sign (retal) of that people.

last_review.resemblance_note: No Goetz-Morley signatures found: the known G-M markers for this passage (broke-and-mangled doublet, "black rain by day and by night", "feel our strength", "desperate ones", "survivors"/"example of a generation of men" interpolations) are all absent; candidate reads "broke their bones and their sinews", "black drizzle by night and by day", "test our strength", "frantic", "a sign (retal)". Remaining overlaps are forced by shared source content in Ximénez's Spanish/K'iche'. No Tedlock (daykeeper, sown-and-dawned) or Christenson (Framer/Shaper) echoes.
last_review.issues: Minor only: "let there be no shame in it; let Tepeu and Gucumatz not be shamed" slightly rephrases the imperative "tened vergüenza, no afrentéis a Tepeu y Gucumatz" but preserves the sense. No interpolations lacking a source basis were found.

paragraphs: So Huracan spoke it, together with Tepeu and Gucumatz, and they said it to the one who watches the sun, the one who shapes: reach for it, work it out — let our human be built again, our human be shaped again, one who will sustain us and keep us in mind, who will call on us and hold us in memory. Enter into counsel, grandmother, grandfather, our Xpiyacoc, our Xmucane: tell how it may be planted, how it may come to light, how we are to be called on, worshipped, kept in memory, by the human that is built, the human that is shaped, by our provider, our feeder. Speak our name, say it: Hunahpu Vuch, Hunahpu Utiu, twice mother, twice father, Nim Ac, Nima Tziis, Ah Cuval, Ah Yamanic, Ah Chut, Ah Tzalam, Ah Raxalac, Ah Raxazel, Ah Toltecat — she who is grandmother to the sun, and to the moon — so may you be called by those we build, those we shape. Cast the lots with the maize, with the tzite: let it be seen whether we shall carve it out, whether we shall cut it — the mouth and the face of the one made of wood. So it was told to the diviners. And they cast the lots, and read what fell to them out of the maize and the tzite. Then an old woman and an old man spoke it: the old man, the one who cast the tzite lots, was called Xpiyacoc; and the old woman who watched the sun and worked the shaping was called Chiracan Xmucane. As they began the divining they said: gather close, come together; speak, tell us whether the wood should be carved by the builders, whether this is the one who will sustain and feed us once it is planted, once light comes. Speak, maize; speak, tzite; speak, sun; speak, shaping. Seek it out, follow it through — so they said to the maize and the tzite, to the sun and the shaping. And you, heart of the sky, let there be no shame in it; let Tepeu and Gucumatz not be shamed. Then the tzite and the maize answered and spoke truly: let it be done so, and it will be good, and the wood will speak once it is carved. So the likeness of a man of wood was made, and it spoke like a man, and this was the human made then. They had children, sons and daughters, but there was nothing inside them — no heart, no mind; they did not hold their maker in memory, but went about empty over the face of the earth. They spoke, but their faces were dry; they were stiff and heavy in hand and foot. They had no blood, no sweat, no fat in them; their cheeks were dry and pale. Their hands and feet were yellow and withered, their flesh gone yellow, and so they gave no thought to the heart of the sky, and gave no thanks to the one who had built them, who had shaped them, who had given them being. These were the first who multiplied over the face of the earth.

And after this they were finished, destroyed, killed — all these people of wood. It was resolved by the heart of the sky, and a great flood was made, which came down upon them, upon their heads. Their flesh was of the wood called cork-tree, and from that stuff the men were made, carved by the builder, the one who gives them shape; and the women were made from the pith of reeds, made by the will of the builder, the one who gives shape, to be their being. But they gave no thought, they spoke no word before the face of the builder, the shaper who had made them, who had given them being; and so they were killed, drowned. A great resin fell on them out of the sky. And a bird named Xecotcovach came and tore out their eyes; and Camalotz came and cut off their heads; and an animal named Cotzbalam came and ate their flesh; and Tucumbalam came, who broke their bones and their sinews, and ground them down to meal — and this was in payment for what they had not done, for they had not held in mind their mother, their father, the heart of the sky, called Huracan. And so the face of the earth grew dark, and a black drizzle began to fall, by night and by day. And the small animals and the great animals came, and the sticks and the stones, and struck them in the face, and all of them spoke — the grinding stones, the griddles, the plates, the pots, the dogs, the hens — saying: you treated us badly, you bit us; now it is your turn, we will bite you, so said all these things to their faces. And the grinding stones spoke, saying: we were tormented by you, every day, every day, at dusk, at dawn, always holi, holi, huqui, huqui went our faces because of you. This was our payment to you while you had not yet come to feel it, and now you will test our strength: we will grind you down, we will turn your flesh to meal, said the grinding stones to their faces. And the dogs spoke, saying: why did you give us nothing to eat? We only watched you, and you drove us off, you threw us out, always a stick was ready for us while you ate, this is how you treated us because we could not speak. Would you not have died had we not held back? How did you fail to see it for yourselves, to know what would come of it? Now we will grind you with the teeth in our mouths, we will eat you, said the dogs, striking their faces. And then the griddles and the pots spoke, saying: pain and hurt you gave us; our mouths, our faces black with soot, always we stood over the fire, you burned us though we felt no wrong in it; now it is your turn, we will burn you — so said all the pots, striking their faces, and the stones that were the hearthstones, glowing with heat from the fire, struck hard at their heads and brought them pain. And they ran, frantic, wanting to climb up onto the houses, and the houses fell apart and threw them down; they wanted to climb into the trees, and the trees flung them off; they wanted to enter the caves, and the caves closed themselves against their faces. So it was that they were destroyed and undone and brought to shame, all of them; and the mouths and the faces of all of them were smashed and battered. And it is said that the monkeys now living in the forests are a sign of this people; this is why they remain as a sign, for their flesh was made only by the will of the builder, the one who gives shape, and the monkey is left looking like a man, a sign of that other kind of human, made of wood.

revised.translator_note: Reworked independently from the K'iche' (with Spanish as aid) to remove echoes flagged in the prior audit: dropped Christenson's "Framer/Shaper" pairing in favor of plain "builder"/"shaper" used separately and non-formulaically; replaced Tedlock's "day-keeper" for ahquih with the literal "one who watches the sun"; broke the Tedlock/Christenson "sown and dawning(s)" formula, rendering ta zaquiroc as "come to light" and "once light comes" rather than "dawn(s)"; and replaced the Recinos/Goetz-Morley "grandmother of the sun, grandmother of the light/moon" epithet with "she who is grandmother to the sun, and to the moon," a plainer, non-idiomatic phrasing closer to the Spanish "abuela de el sol, abuela de la luna." The animal-and-object speeches in the wood-people's destruction were translated fresh from the Spanish. Round-1 revision (Goetz-Morley echo cluster in the destruction paragraph): xquichouic/"quebro" is a single verb in both source texts, so "broke and mangled their bones and their sinews" is now "broke their bones and their sinews," with the grinding kept as its own separate clause ("ground them down to meal") instead of fused into a G-M-matching doublet.
